CFS Enters., Inc. v CG & J Realty, LLC 
 2026 NY Slip Op 05929 
 October 14, 2026 
 Appellate Division, Second Department 
 Published by New York State Law Reporting Bureau pursuant to Judiciary Law § 431. 
 This decision is uncorrected and subject to revision before publication in the Official Reports. 

 CFS Enterprises, Inc., respondent, 
 v 
 CG & J Realty, LLC, appellant, et al., defendants. 

 Supreme Court of the State of New York, Appellate Division, Second Judicial Department 
 Decided on October 14, 2026 
 2024-13568, (Index No. 703051/23) 
 Francesca E. Connolly, J.P. 
 Valerie Brathwaite Nelson 
 Barry E. Warhit 
 James P. McCormack, JJ. 

 Redmond Law PLLC, New York, NY (Jennifer Redmond of counsel), for appellant. 
 Chan Vitanza LLP, New York, NY (Henry C. Chan, Virginie Brizon, George Paliogiannis, and Deema Hassan of counsel), for respondent. 

 [*1] 
 DECISION & ORDER 
 In an action, inter alia, to foreclose a mechanic's lien, the defendant CG & J Realty, LLC, appeals from an order of the Supreme Court, Queens County (Cassandra A. Johnson, J.), dated October 24, 2024. The order, insofar as appealed from, denied the motion of the defendant CG & J Realty, LLC, to vacate and cancel a bond and to dismiss the cause of action to foreclose the mechanic's lien insofar as asserted against it. 
 ORDERED that the order is affirmed insofar as appealed from, with costs. 
 On November 7, 2022, the plaintiff filed a notice under the Lien Law, claiming that it had a lien on certain real property located in Queens (hereinafter the premises) that was owned by the defendant CG & J Realty, LLC (hereinafter the defendant). In February 2023, the plaintiff commenced this action against, among others, the defendant, asserting, inter alia, a cause of action to foreclose the mechanic's lien. In April 2023, the defendant filed a notice of discharge of public improvements lien bond and posted a bond pursuant to Lien Law § 19 to discharge the lien (hereinafter the Section 19 bond). In July 2023, Century Construction Group Corp. filed a bond pursuant to Lien Law § 37 (hereinafter the Section 37 bond) and moved to discharge "all liens and claims that may be filed against [the premises]." In an order dated October 10, 2023, the Supreme Court discharged all liens and claims against the premises, setting forth that the Section 37 bond "shall supersede all prior bonds that discharged any liens and claims" against the premises. 
 Subsequently, by order to show cause, the defendant moved pursuant to Lien Law § 59 to vacate and cancel the Section 19 bond and to dismiss the cause of action to foreclose the mechanic's lien insofar as asserted against it. The plaintiff opposed the defendant's motion. In an order dated October 24, 2024, the Supreme Court, among other things, denied the defendant's motion. The defendant appeals. 
 "Mechanic's liens have their derivation entirely in statutory law, existing neither in common law nor in equity" ( Umbaugh Bldrs. v Parr Co. of Suffolk , 86 Misc 2d 1036 , 1037 [Sup Ct, Suffolk County]). As such, "[s]trict compliance with the statutory requirements is mandated and the court does not have discretion to excuse noncompliance" ( Matter of EK Mt Kisco, LLC v Arcon Constr. Group, Inc. , 138 AD3d 1118 , 1118-1119 [internal quotation marks omitted]; see Matter of [*2] HMB Acquisition Corp. v F & K Supply , 209 AD2d 412, 412 ). 
 Lien Law § 59 provides, in pertinent part, that "[a] mechanic's lien notice of which has been filed on real property or a bond given to discharge the same may be vacated . . . by an order of a court of record. Before such order shall be granted, a notice shall be served upon the lienor, either personally or by leaving it [at] his [or her] last known place of residence, with a person of suitable age, with directions to deliver it to the lienor." 
 Here, the defendant failed to satisfy the requirements of Lien Law § 59, as the defendant merely filed on NYSCEF the order to show cause informing the plaintiff of the defendant's intention to vacate the bond and did not personally serve it on the plaintiff or leave it with a person of suitable age and discretion at the plaintiff's last known place of residence ( see Matter of Eastchester Church Inc. , 44 Misc 3d 653, 654 [Sup Ct, Bronx County]). 
 Accordingly, the Supreme Court properly denied the defendant's motion to vacate the bond and to dismiss the cause of action to foreclose the mechanic's lien insofar as asserted against it. 
 The plaintiff seeks costs in the form of reimbursement of reasonable attorneys' fees and expenses incurred in defending this appeal pursuant to 22 NYCRR 130-1.1(c), alleging that the defendant's conduct in taking this appeal was frivolous. 
 "A court, in its discretion, may award to any party or attorney in any civil action or proceeding before the court . . . costs in the form of reimbursement for actual expenses reasonably incurred and reasonable attorney's fees, resulting from frivolous conduct" ( U.S. Bank N.A. v Tait , 234 AD3d 889 , 891 [internal quotation marks omitted]; see Curet v DeKalb Realty, LLC , 127 AD3d 914, 916 ). "Although the advancement of a meritless position may serve as the basis for a finding of frivolity, the standard for such a showing is high: the rule provides that a position will be deemed frivolous only where it is completely without merit in law and cannot be supported by a reasonable argument for an extension, modification or reversal of existing law" ( Hossain v Hossain , 243 AD3d 894 , 896 [internal quotation marks omitted]; see West Hempstead Water Dist. v Buckeye Pipeline Co., L.P. , 152 AD3d 558, 558-559 ). "A party seeking . . . an award of an attorney's fee pursuant to 22 NYCRR 130.1.1[ ] has the burden of demonstrating that the conduct of the opposing party was frivolous within the meaning of" 22 NYCRR 130-1.1(c) ( Matter of Miller v Miller , 96 AD3d 943, 944 ). 
 Here, the plaintiff failed to establish that the defendant's conduct was frivolous within the meaning of 22 NYCRR 130-1.1(c) ( see Zhuoya Luo v Wensheng Wang , 176 AD3d 1016 , 1018). 
 The parties' remaining contentions either are without merit or need not be reached in light of our determination. 
 CONNOLLY, J.P., BRATHWAITE NELSON, WARHIT and MCCORMACK, JJ., concur.

leads.caseName: Deutsche Bank Natl. Trust Co. v. Merrill
leads.court: Appellate Division of the Supreme Court of the State of New York
leads.text:
Deutsche Bank Natl. Trust Co. v Merrill 
 2026 NY Slip Op 05933 
 October 14, 2026 
 Appellate Division, Second Department 
 Published by New York State Law Reporting Bureau pursuant to Judiciary Law § 431. 
 This decision is uncorrected and subject to revision before publication in the Official Reports. 

 Deutsche Bank National Trust Company, etc., appellant, 
 v 
 Pamela Merrill, respondent, et al., defendants. 

 Supreme Court of the State of New York, Appellate Division, Second Judicial Department 
 Decided on October 14, 2026 
 2025-01447, (Index No. 711920/23) 
 Lara J. Genovesi, J.P. 
 William G. Ford 
 Helen Voutsinas 
 Donna-Marie E. Golia, JJ. 

 McCarter & English, LLP, New York, NY (Adam M. Swanson and Jessie D. Bonaros of counsel), for appellant. 
 Mobilization for Justice, Inc., New York, NY (Tiffany Liston and Liana Goff of counsel), for respondent. 

 [*1] 
 DECISION & ORDER 
 In an action to foreclose a mortgage, the plaintiff appeals from an order of the Supreme Court, Queens County (Tracy Catapano-Fox, J.), entered December 30, 2024. The order, insofar as appealed from, denied the plaintiff's motion, inter alia, for summary judgment on the complaint insofar as asserted against the defendant Pamela Merrill and for an order of reference, and granted those branches of that defendant's cross-motion which were for summary judgment dismissing the complaint insofar as asserted against her and on her counterclaim pursuant to RPAPL 1501(4) to cancel and discharge of record the mortgage. 
 ORDERED that the order is affirmed insofar as appealed from, with costs. 
 On March 30, 2005, the defendant Pamela Merrill executed a note in the sum of $164,800 in favor of GreenPoint Mortgage Funding, Inc. The note was secured by a mortgage on certain real property located in Laurelton. Merrill allegedly defaulted on her payment obligations under the note in July 2009. By assignment of mortgage dated October 29, 2009, the mortgage was assigned to the plaintiff. 
 On November 19, 2009, the plaintiff commenced an action against Merrill, among others, to foreclose the mortgage (hereinafter the 2009 action). The plaintiff elected in the complaint "to call due the entire amount secured by the mortgage." Merrill interposed an answer to the complaint. In November 2015, the plaintiff moved to discontinue the 2009 action and to cancel the notice of pendency. In an order dated March 23, 2016, and entered April 11, 2016, the Supreme Court granted the plaintiff's motion. 
 On April 5, 2016, the plaintiff commenced a second action to foreclose the mortgage against Merrill, among others (hereinafter the 2016 action). In an order dated January 6, 2023, the Supreme Court, inter alia, directed dismissal of the complaint in the 2016 action for failure to comply with RPAPL 1304. 
 On June 8, 2023, the plaintiff commenced this action to foreclose the mortgage [*2] against Merrill, among others. Merrill interposed an answer in which she asserted, among other things, an affirmative defense alleging that the action was barred by the statute of limitations and a counterclaim pursuant to RPAPL 1501(4) to cancel and discharge of record the mortgage. The plaintiff moved, inter alia, for summary judgment on the complaint insofar as asserted against Merrill and for an order of reference. Merrill cross-moved, among other things, for summary judgment dismissing the complaint insofar as asserted against her as time-barred and on her counterclaim pursuant to RPAPL 1501(4) to cancel and discharge of record the mortgage in light of the enactment of the Foreclosure Abuse Prevention Act (FAPA) (L 2022, ch 821 [eff Dec. 30, 2022]). In an order entered December 30, 2024, the Supreme Court, inter alia, denied the plaintiff's motion and granted those branches of Merrill's cross-motion which were for summary judgment dismissing the complaint insofar as asserted against her and on her counterclaim pursuant to RPAPL 1501(4) to cancel and discharge of record the mortgage. The plaintiff appeals. 
 "An action to foreclose a mortgage is governed by a six-year statute of limitations" ( U.S. Bank N.A. v Santos , 218 AD3d 827, 828 ; see CPLR 213[4]; Lubonty v U.S. Bank N.A. , 34 NY3d 250 , 261; U.S. Bank N.A. v Singh , 247 AD3d 816 , 818; FV-1, Inc. v Palaguachi , 234 AD3d 818 , 820). "[E]ven if a mortgage is payable in installments, once a mortgage debt is accelerated, the entire amount is due and the statute of limitations begins to run on the entire debt" ( Bank of N.Y. Mellon v Mor , 201 AD3d 691, 694 ; see U.S. Bank N.A. v Singh , 247 AD3d at 818; U.S. Bank Trust, N.A. v Boreshesky , 241 AD3d 1385 , 1386; Citimortgage, Inc. v Gunn , 234 AD3d 922 ). "The entire mortgage debt will be deemed to have been accelerated by, as relevant here, the commencement of a mortgage foreclosure action in which the complaint seeks payment of the full outstanding loan balance" ( U.S. Bank N.A. v Connor , 204 AD3d 861, 863 ; see U.S. Bank N.A. v Singh , 247 AD3d at 818; U.S. Bank Trust, N.A. v Boreshesky , 241 AD3d at 1386-1387). 
 CPLR 203(h), as amended by FAPA, provides, in relevant part, that once a cause of action to foreclose a mortgage has accrued, no party may, in form or effect, unilaterally revive or reset the accrual thereof, or otherwise purport to effect a unilateral extension of the statute of limitations ( see U.S. Bank N.A. v Singh , 247 AD3d at 818; U.S. Bank Trust, N.A. v Horowitz , 238 AD3d 1093 ; FV-1, Inc. v Palaguachi , 234 AD3d at 821). Moreover, FAPA amended CPLR 3217(e) to provide, in relevant part, that the voluntary discontinuance of a foreclosure action shall not toll, extend, revive, or reset the statute of limitations, unless expressly prescribed by statute ( see U.S. Bank N.A. v Singh , 247 AD3d at 818; FV-1, Inc. v Palaguachi , 234 AD3d at 821). 
 Pursuant to RPAPL 1501(4), a person having an estate or interest in real property subject to a mortgage may maintain an action to secure the cancellation and discharge of record of the mortgage and to adjudge the estate or interest free of it, if the applicable statute of limitations for commencing a foreclosure action has expired ( see U.S. Bank N.A. v Singh , 247 AD3d at 818; U.S. Bank N.A. v Medianik , 223 AD3d 935 , 938; Ditmid Holdings, LLC v JPMorgan Chase Bank, N.A. , 180 AD3d 1002, 1003 ). 
 Here, Merrill established, prima facie, that the six-year statute of limitations began to run in November 2009 when the plaintiff commenced the 2009 action and elected in the complaint to call due the entire amount secured by the mortgage ( see U.S. Bank N.A. v Singh , 247 AD3d at 818; HSBC Bank USA, N.A. v Corrales , 224 AD3d 816 , 818). Merrill further demonstrated that this action was commenced in June 2023, more than six years later ( see CPLR 213[4]; U.S. Bank N.A. v Singh , 247 AD3d at 818; U.S. Bank Trust, N.A. v Boreshesky , 241 AD3d at 1388; Citimortgage, Inc. v Gunn , 234 AD3d at 923; U.S. Bank N.A. v Doura , 204 AD3d 721, 723 ). 
 In opposition, the plaintiff failed to raise a triable issue of fact. Contrary to the plaintiff's contention, applying FAPA, its voluntary discontinuance of the 2009 action did not revive or reset the statute of limitations ( see CPLR 203[h]; 3217[e]; IPA Asset Mgt., LLC v HSBC Bank USA, N.A. , 234 AD3d 948 , 950; Wells Fargo Bank, N.A. v Edwards , 231 AD3d 1189 , 1193). Moreover, since the 2016 action was untimely commenced, the plaintiff's contention that it could avail itself of the savings provision contained in CPLR 205-a to render this action timely is without merit. 
 Furthermore, there is no merit to the plaintiff's contention that FAPA does not apply retroactively ( see Van Dyke v U.S. Bank, N.A. , 45 NY3d 461 , 474; Article 13 LLC v Ponce De Leon Fed. Bank , 45 NY3d 441 , 451-453). The plaintiff's arguments challenging FAPA's constitutionality are without merit ( see Van Dyke v U.S. Bank, N.A. , 45 NY3d 461 ; Article 13 LLC v Ponce De Leon Fed. Bank , 45 NY3d 441 ; Wilmington Sav. Fund Socy., FSB v Lozowski , 245 AD3d 986 ; Deutsche Bank Natl. Trust Co. v Dagrin , 233 AD3d 1065 , 1069-1071). 
 Accordingly, the Supreme Court properly granted those branches of Merrill's cross-motion which were for summary judgment dismissing the complaint insofar as asserted against her and on her counterclaim pursuant to RPAPL 1501(4) to cancel and discharge of record the mortgage, and properly denied the plaintiff's motion, among other things, for summary judgment on the complaint insofar as asserted against Merrill and for an order of reference. 
 GENOVESI, J.P., FORD, VOUTSINAS and GOLIA, JJ., concur.

 Darrell M. Joseph 
 Clerk of the Court

leads.caseName: Matter of Hunter v. Zoning Bd. of Appeals of the Town of Islip
leads.court: Appellate Division of the Supreme Court of the State of New York
leads.text:
Matter of Hunter v Zoning Bd. of Appeals of the Town of Islip 
 2026 NY Slip Op 05953 
 October 14, 2026 
 Appellate Division, Second Department 
 Published by New York State Law Reporting Bureau pursuant to Judiciary Law § 431. 
 This decision is uncorrected and subject to revision before publication in the Official Reports. 

 In the Matter of Michael L. Hunter III, et al., appellants, 
 v 
 Zoning Board of Appeals of the Town of Islip, respondent. 

 Supreme Court of the State of New York, Appellate Division, Second Judicial Department 
 Decided on October 14, 2026 
 2024-10955, (Index No. 604535/24) 
 Lara J. Genovesi, J.P. 
 William G. Ford 
 Helen Voutsinas 
 Donna-Marie E. Golia, JJ. 

 Sahn Ward Braff Coschignano PLLC, Uniondale, NY (Michael H. Sahn, Joseph R. Bjarnson, and Ralph Branciforte of counsel), for appellants. 
 William F. Garbarino, Town Attorney, Islip, NY (Jordan L. Lite and Joseph V. DeMaggio of counsel), for respondent. 

 [*1] 
 DECISION & ORDER 
 In a proceeding pursuant to CPLR article 78 to review so much of a determination of the Zoning Board of Appeals of the Town of Islip dated January 23, 2024, as, after a hearing, denied so much of the petitioners' application as was for certain area variances, the petitioners appeal from a judgment of the Supreme Court, Suffolk County (Christopher Modelewski, J.), dated September 6, 2024. The judgment denied the petition and dismissed the proceeding. 
 ORDERED that the judgment is affirmed, with costs. 
 In January 2021, the Zoning Board of Appeals of the Town of Islip (hereinafter the ZBA) granted the petitioners' application for a permit to renovate their existing detached garage, which had been constructed prior to the enactment of the zoning laws. Thereafter, the petitioners demolished the detached garage and constructed a new structure. In a letter dated October 6, 2022, the Town of Islip Building Division, Zoning Department, informed the petitioners that their detached garage had been reviewed and that the newly constructed garage did not conform with the previously granted permit. In November 2022, the petitioners applied to the ZBA, inter alia, for area variances related to their newly constructed garage. 
 After a hearing, the ZBA denied so much of the petitioners' application as was for area variances related to their newly constructed garage. The petitioners commenced this proceeding pursuant to CPLR article 78 to review that portion of the ZBA's determination. By judgment dated September 6, 2024, the Supreme Court denied the petition and dismissed the proceeding. The petitioners appeal. 
 Local zoning boards have broad discretion in considering applications for variances, and judicial review is limited to determining whether the action taken by the board was illegal, arbitrary, or an abuse of discretion ( see Matter of Kami Holding Corp. v Zoning Bd. of Appeals of the Vil. of Westbury , 223 AD3d 811 , 812; Matter of Carnelian Farms, LLC v Leventhal , 151 AD3d 844, 845 ). The determination of a local zoning board is entitled to great deference, and will be set aside only if it is illegal, arbitrary and capricious, or irrational ( see Matter of Carella v Zoning Bd. [*2] of Appeals of the Town of Ramapo , 235 AD3d 974 , 975; Matter of Gabriele v Zoning Bd. of Appeals of the Town of Eastchester , 228 AD3d 659 , 660). 
 The determination of the ZBA was not arbitrary and capricious. When a zoning board of appeals makes a determination of whether to grant an area variance to an applicant, the zoning board is required to engage in a balancing test, weighing the benefit of the grant to the applicant against the detriment to the health, safety, and welfare of the neighborhood or community if the variance is granted ( see Matter of Massian v Board of Zoning Appeals of the Town of Brookhaven , 210 AD3d 984, 985 ; Matter of Morris Motel, LLC v DeChance , 199 AD3d 687, 688 ). The zoning board must consider the following factors when making its determination: "whether (1) an undesirable change will be produced in the character of the neighborhood or a detriment to nearby properties will be created by the granting of the area variance; (2) the benefit sought by the applicant can be achieved by some method, feasible for the applicant to pursue, other than an area variance; (3) the requested area variance is substantial; (4) the proposed variance will have an adverse effect or impact on the physical or environmental conditions in the neighborhood or district; and (5) the alleged difficulty was self-created" ( Matter of Bernstein v Putnam Val. Zoning Bd. of Appeals , 191 AD3d 779, 781 ; see Matter of D.P.R. Scrap Metal, Inc. v Board of Zoning Appeals of Town of N. Hempstead , 187 AD3d 748, 749 ). 
 Here, the record demonstrates that the ZBA engaged in the required balancing test and considered the relevant statutory factors. The area variances sought by the petitioners were substantial in nature ( see Matter of Pecoraro v Board of Appeals of Town of Hempstead , 2 NY3d 608, 614 ; Matter of Bonadonna v Board of Zoning Appeals of the Inc. Vil. of Upper Brookville , 220 AD3d 855, 858 ). The evidence before the ZBA also supported its conclusions that granting the requested area variances would produce an undesirable change in the character of the neighborhood ( see Matter of Seaview Assn. of Fire Is., NY, Inc. v Town of Islip Zoning Bd. of Appeals , 221 AD3d 717, 719 ; Matter of Nataro v DeChance , 149 AD3d 1081, 1082 ). Further, as the ZBA determined that no similar variances had been granted, it was permitted to consider the possibility that granting the requested variances could set a negative precedent within the area ( see Matter of Seaview Assn. of Fire Is., NY, Inc. v Town of Islip Zoning Bd. of Appeals , 221 AD3d at 719 ). Moreover, the ZBA properly found that any hardship was self-created ( see Matter of Kami Holding Corp. v Zoning Bd. of Appeals of the Vil. of Westbury , 223 AD3d at 813; Matter of Latuga v Giannadeo , 140 AD3d 771, 772 ). 
 Finally, the petitioners' contention that so much of the ZBA's determination as denied so much of their application as was for area variances related to their newly constructed garage was arbitrary and capricious because the ZBA had previously granted their application in 2021 regarding their original garage is without merit, as they failed to establish that the ZBA reached a different result on essentially the same facts ( see Matter of Harris v Zoning Bd. of Appeals of Town of Carmel , 137 AD3d 1130, 1132 ; Matter of Christian Airmen, Inc. v Town of Newstead Zoning Bd. of Appeals , 115 AD3d 1319 , 1322). Therefore, so much of the ZBA's determination as denied so much of the petitioners' application as was for area variances related to their newly constructed garage was rational and not arbitrary and capricious ( see Matter of Kami Holding Corp. v Zoning Bd. of Appeals of the Vil. of Westbury , 223 AD3d at 813; Matter of Seaview Assn. of Fire Is., NY, Inc. v Town of Islip Zoning Bd. of Appeals , 221 AD3d at 718-719 ). 
 GENOVESI, J.P., FORD, VOUTSINAS and GOLIA, JJ., concur.

 Darrell M. Joseph 
 Clerk of the Court

leads.text:
Matter of VN Prop., Inc. v Byrne 
 2026 NY Slip Op 05961 
 October 14, 2026 
 Appellate Division, Second Department 
 Published by New York State Law Reporting Bureau pursuant to Judiciary Law § 431. 
 This decision is uncorrected and subject to revision before publication in the Official Reports. 

 In the Matter of VN Property, Inc., appellant, 
 v 
 Rita Byrne, etc., et al., respondents. 

 Supreme Court of the State of New York, Appellate Division, Second Judicial Department 
 Decided on October 14, 2026 
 2024-08064, (Index No. 615288/23) 
 Mark C. Dillon, J.P. 
 Paul Wooten 
 Lourdes M. Ventura 
 Lisa S. Ottley, JJ. 

 Andrew J. Levitt, P.C., Melville, NY, for appellant. 
 Kendric Law Group P.C., Cold Spring Harbor, NY (Christopher Kendric of counsel), for respondents. 

 [*1] 
 DECISION & ORDER 
 In a proceeding pursuant to CPLR article 78 to review a determination of the Zoning Board of Appeals of the Town of Oyster Bay dated July 20, 2023, which, after a hearing, denied the petitioner's application for certain area variances, the petitioner appeals from an order and judgment (one paper) of the Supreme Court, Nassau County (Conrad D. Singer, J.), dated April 29, 2024. The order and judgment, inter alia, denied the petition and, in effect, dismissed the proceeding. 
 ORDERED that the order and judgment is affirmed, with costs. 
 The petitioner, the owner of a residential property located in Hicksville, applied to the Zoning Board of Appeals of the Town of Oyster Bay (hereinafter the ZBA) for area variances, inter alia, for certain extensions to the second floor. Specifically, the petitioner sought variances, among other things, for gross floor area, minimum and total side yard setbacks, and roof pitch. After a hearing, the ZBA denied the application, and the petitioner commenced this proceeding pursuant to CPLR article 78 to review the ZBA's determination. By order and judgment dated April 29, 2024, the Supreme Court, inter alia, denied the petition and, in effect, dismissed the proceeding. The petitioner appeals. 
 Local zoning boards have broad discretion in considering variance applications, and judicial review is limited to determining whether the action taken by the board was affected by an error of law, arbitrary and capricious, or an abuse of discretion ( see id. § 7803[3]; Matter of Bonadonna v Board of Zoning Appeals of the Inc. Vil. of Upper Brookville , 220 AD3d 855, 856-857 ; Matter of White Birch Circle Realty Corp. v DeChance , 212 AD3d 729, 730 ). Where, as here, a zoning board's determination is made after a public hearing, its determination should be upheld if it has a rational basis and is supported by evidence in the record ( see Matter of Bonadonna v Board of Zoning Appeals of the Inc. Vil. of Upper Brookville , 220 AD3d at 857 ; Matter of Ogden Land Dev., LLC v Zoning Bd. of Appeals of Vil. of Scarsdale , 121 AD3d 695, 696 ). 
 In considering an application for area variances, Town Law § 267-b(3)(b) requires a zoning board to engage in a balancing test, weighing the benefit to the petitioner against the detriment to the health, safety, and welfare of the neighborhood or community if the area variances are granted ( see Matter of White Birch Circle Realty Corp. v DeChance , 212 AD3d at 730 ). In particular, a zoning board must consider: "(1) whether an undesirable change will be produced in the character of the neighborhood or a detriment to nearby properties will be created by the granting [*2] of the area variance; (2) whether the benefit sought by the applicant can be achieved by some method, feasible for the applicant to pursue, other than an area variance; (3) whether the requested area variance is substantial; (4) whether the proposed variance will have an adverse effect or impact on the physical or environmental conditions in the neighborhood or district; and (5) whether the alleged difficulty was self-created, which consideration shall be relevant to the decision of the board of appeals, but shall not necessarily preclude the granting of the area variance" (Town Law § 267-b[3][b]). The zoning board, in applying the balancing test, is not required to justify its determination with supporting evidence for each of the five statutory factors as long as its determination balancing the relevant considerations is rational ( see Matter of Humphreys v Somers Zoning Bd. of Appeals , 206 AD3d 1000 , 1002). 
 Here, contrary to the petitioner's contention, the record reflects that the ZBA engaged in the requisite balancing of interests and considered the appropriate factors pursuant to Town Law § 267-b(3)(b) in determining the petitioner's application, and the ZBA's determination had a rational basis and was supported by the record ( see Matter of Maldonado v Board of Appeals of the Inc. Vil. of Val. Stream , 244 AD3d 1210 , 1211-1212; Matter of White Birch Circle Realty Corp. v DeChance , 212 AD3d at 731 ). The ZBA rationally concluded, inter alia, that the requested variances were substantial, that granting the variances would produce an undesirable change in the character of the neighborhood, and that the petitioner's alleged hardship was self-created. 
 Thus, the ZBA's determination was not affected by an error of law, arbitrary and capricious, or an abuse of discretion. Accordingly, the Supreme Court properly denied the petition and, in effect, dismissed the proceeding. 
 The petitioner's remaining contention is without merit. 
 DILLON, J.P., WOOTEN, VENTURA and OTTLEY, JJ., concur.

DILLARD, P. J.,
GOBEIL and PIPKIN, JJ.

October 14, 2026
In the Court of Appeals of Georgia
A26A1018. JENNINGS v. ROMULUS INVESTMENTS, LLC et al.
DILLARD, Presiding Judge.
William Jennings suffered serious, permanent injuries when a massive tree on
his next door neighbor’s property fell and crushed the house he was leasing from
Romulus Investments while he was still inside. Jennings filed suit against Romulus and
its two owners, Christopher Alvey and Wendell Rhodes,1 claiming the lease and
statutory law imposed duties on Romulus to protect him against the hazard posed by
the tree—even though it did not sit on the leased property. Romulus moved for
summary judgment, which the trial court granted. Jennings contends the court erred
1 For the sake of clarity, we refer to Romulus Investments, Christopher Alvey,
and Wendell Rhodes collectively as “Romulus” throughout this opinion.
in doing so, arguing that genuine issues of material fact remain as to whether (1)
Romulus owed a duty under the lease; (2) it owed a duty under OCGA § 51-3-1; (3) it
owed a duty under OCGA § 44-7-14; and (4) attorney fees and punitive damages were
warranted. For the following reasons, we reverse.2
Viewed in the light most favorable to Jennings (i.e., the nonmoving party),3 the
record shows that Alvey and Rhodes formed Romulus to buy residential properties and
lease them. Toward that end, on April 2, 2021, Romulus purchased the property
located at 10 Circle Drive in Lindale, Georgia. And on April 5, 2021, Romulus entered
into a lease with Jennings for that property. Under the lease, Jennings paid $650 in
monthly rent (in person) to Romulus’s office in Rome. Significantly, the lease provided
that the “[l]andlord shall maintain the property at all times ... . Tenant must call
landlord and notify him of any problems immediately and the Landlord will have the
problem repaired as soon as possible.” The lease also added that “[s]ubject to
Tenant’s consent (within a reasonable time period), the Landlord shall have the right
2 Oral argument was held on May 5, 2026, and is archived on the Court’s
website. See Court of Appeals of the State of Georgia, Oral Argument, Case No.
A26A1018 (May 5, 2026), available at https://vimeo.com/1191278959.
3 See, e.g., Swanson v. Tackling, 335 Ga. App. 810, 810 (783 SE2d 167) (2016).
2
to inspect the premises for suspected damage or poor housekeeping habits, to show
property to perspective buyers or any other person for business purposes.”
Additionally, in a paragraph titled “Hazards,” the lease provided that “[a]ny known
safety hazards are to be made known to Landlord ASAP.” 
Right next door to the leased property—10 Circle Drive—is 8 Circle Drive, an
empty lot. This lot is owned by Jennings’s neighbor, Misty Carroll, who purchased the
property from another neighbor, David Jordan, who resided across the street from
Jennings at 9 Circle Drive. Near the boundary between 10 Circle Drive and 8 Circle
Drive was a massive oak tree estimated to be over 80 years old. And while the tree’s
trunk sat on 8 Circle Drive, some of its large limbs and branches extended well over the
10 Circle Drive property line—even over the house Jennings rented from Romulus.
Unfortunately, at least two times after Jennings began renting 10 Circle Drive, large
branches from the tree on 8 Circle Drive fell on the house. And sometime in the spring
of 2022, lightning struck the tree, causing a large limb to fall on Jennings’s truck and
damage it. Jennings notified Romulus—via Alvey—about the tree’s limbs falling on
the property and his truck. In doing so, Jennings told Alvey that he believed the tree
3
was decaying and dangerous and someone “needed to come out and look at it.”
Jennings also shared his concerns with others in Romulus’s office when he dropped off
his rent check on the first of each month. 
Despite these warnings, neither Romulus nor Carroll—the owner of 8 Circle
Drive—ever inspected the tree to assess its health or undertook any measures to
remove the tree or its limbs that were overhanging on to the 10 Circle Drive property
(where Jennings resided). Moreover, Romulus and Carroll apparently never
communicated with each other about removing the tree or the overhanging limbs.
Tragically, around noon on July 14, 2022, the tree fell on the 10 Circle Drive house,
crashing through the roof and pinning Jennings underneath a large part of the trunk and
debris. Fire department and emergency medical personnel quickly arrived on the
scene, but it took nearly two hours before Jennings was rescued from the destroyed
home. And because of the accident, Jennings suffered a serious injury to his spinal
cord, which rendered him permanently paralyzed from the chest down. 
Later on, Jennings filed suit in the Superior Court of Floyd County against
Alvey, Rhodes, and Romulus, alleging claims for breach of the lease agreement,
4
premises liability, failure to keep the premises in good repair and fit for habitation, and
common-law negligence. And along with compensatory damages, Jennings sought
attorney fees and punitive damages. Romulus filed answers, and discovery ensued. At
the end of discovery, Romulus moved for summary judgment as to all of Jennings’s
claims, which the trial court granted after a hearing. 
Jennings appealed, and in an unpublished opinion, we vacated the trial court’s
ruling—without addressing the merits of Jennings’s arguments—and remanded the
case with direction that the court clarify the basis for granting summary judgment as
to the breach-of-lease claim because it had not been mentioned in the order.4 After
remand, the court again granted Romulus’s motion for summary judgment, issuing an
identical order but with an added section addressing Jennings’s breach-of-lease claim.
This appeal follows.
Summary judgment is proper if “the pleadings, depositions, answers to
interrogatories, and admissions on file, together with the affidavits, if any, show that
there is no genuine issue as to any material fact and that the moving party is entitled
4 See Jennings v. Romulus Investments, LLC et al., Case No. A25A1111 (decided
November 3, 2025) (unpublished opinion).
5
to a judgment as a matter of law.”5 Importantly, if the movant meets this burden, the
nonmovant “cannot rest on its pleadings, but rather must point to specific evidence
giving rise to a triable issue.”6 And speculation which “raises merely a conjecture or
possibility is not sufficient to create even an inference of fact for consideration on
summary judgment.”7 Moreover, if summary judgment is granted, it enjoys no
presumption of correctness on appeal, and an appellate court must satisfy itself that the
requirements of OCGA § 9-11-56(c) have been met.8 Importantly, in conducting this
de novo review, we are charged with “viewing the evidence, and all reasonable
conclusions and inferences drawn from the evidence, in the light most favorable to the
5 OCGA § 9-11-56(c). See Swanson, 335 Ga. App. at 811 (explaining that
summary judgment is appropriate when “the moving party can show that there is no
genuine issue of material fact and that the movant is entitled to judgment as a matter
of law” (punctuation omitted)).
6 Handberry v. Manning Forestry Servs., LLC, 353 Ga. App. 150, 151–52 (836
SE2d 545) (2019) (punctuation omitted).
7 Id. at 152 (punctuation omitted).
8 See Cowart v. Widener, 287 Ga. 622, 624(1)(a) (697 SE2d 779) (2010)
(“Summary judgments enjoy no presumption of correctness on appeal, and an
appellate court must satisfy itself de novo that the requirements of OCGA § 9-11-56(c)
have been met.”).
6
nonmovant.”9 With these guiding principles in mind, we turn now to Jennings’s claims
of error.
1. Jennings first contends the trial court erred in granting summary judgment as
to his claims that Romulus owed a duty under the lease and an implied warranty of
habitability to protect against the hazard posed by the oak tree. We agree.
The construction of a lease—or any other contract—is “a question of law for
the court,”10 involving the following three analytical steps:
The first step is to decide whether the language of the contract is clear
and unambiguous. If so, the contract is enforced according to its plain
terms, and the contract alone is looked to for meaning. Second, if the
language of the contract is ambiguous in some respect, the rules of
contract construction must be applied by the court to resolve the
ambiguity. And finally, if ambiguity remains after applying the rules of
9 Benefield v. Tominich, 308 Ga. App. 605, 607(1) (708 SE2d 563) (2011)
(punctuation omitted). Accord Swanson, 335 Ga. App. at 810.
10 Shields v. RDM, LLC, 355 Ga. App. 409, 413(1) (844 SE2d 297) (2020)
(punctuation omitted). See Gleaton & Assocs., Inc. v. Cornelius, 366 Ga. App. 712,
715(1) (884 SE2d 103) (2023) (“The construction of the provisions of a lease is
generally a question for the court to determine as a matter of law.” (punctuation
omitted)).
7
construction, the issue of what the ambiguous language means and what
the parties intended must be resolved by a jury.11
The cardinal rule of contract construction is, of course, “to ascertain the intention of
the parties, as set out in the language of the contract.”12 And when the language of a
contract is plain and unambiguous, “judicial construction is not only unnecessary but
forbidden.”13
Here, the lease agreement provides that the “[l]andlord shall maintain the
property at all times ... [and the] [t]enant must call landlord and notify him of any
problems immediately and the [l]andlord will have the problem repaired as soon as
possible.” Importantly, the term “maintain” in this context is defined as “[t]o keep
11 Shields, 355 Ga. App. at 413(1) (punctuation omitted). Accord Bd. of Cmm’rs
of Crisp Cty. v. City Cmm’rs of the City of Cordele, 315 Ga. App. 696, 699 (727 SE2d
524) (2012).
12 Shields, 355 Ga. App. at 413(1) (punctuation omitted). Accord Stanley v. Gov’t
Emps. Ins. Co., 344 Ga. App. 342, 344(1) (810 SE2d 179) (2018).
13 SPI Holdco, LLC v. Mookerji, 361 Ga. App. 449, 453(1) (864 SE2d 633) (2021)
(punctuation omitted).
8
up, preserve, cause to continue in being (a state of things, a condition, an activity, etc.);
to keep vigorous, effective, or unimpaired; to guard from loss or deterioration.”14
In addition to the language of the lease, the Supreme Court of Georgia has held
that
[a] landlord is subject to liability for physical harm caused ... by a
dangerous condition existing before or arising after the tenant has taken
possession, if he has failed to exercise reasonable care to repair the
condition and the existence of the condition is in violation of ... an implied
warranty of habitability ... or a duty created by statute or administrative
regulation.15
Indeed, far from being a recent development, our Supreme Court has explained that
the General Assembly long ago rejected traditional property law conceptions of
landlord-tenant law, in which a lessor grants and a lessee acquires an estate in
14 Oxford English Dictionary Online, Maintain (verb) (II.7.a),
https://doi.org/10.1093/OED/3208186595 (last visited October 13, 2026).
15 Thompson v. Crownover, 259 Ga. 126, 129(3) (381 SE2d 283) (1989)
(punctuation omitted). Accord Bastien v. Metro. Park Lake Assocs., L.P., 209 Ga. App.
881, 882 (434 SE2d 736) (1993); Restatement of Law (Second) of Property, Land. &
Ten. § 17.6 (1977). See also OCGA § 44-7-13(b) (“Any contract, lease, license, or
similar agreement, oral or written, for the use or rental of real property as a dwelling
place is deemed to include a provision that the premises is fit for human habitation.”).
9
land—instead championing a unique-at-the-time requirement that a “landlord must
keep the premises in repair and is liable for all substantial improvements placed upon
them by his consent.”16

leads.court: Court of Appeals for the Third Circuit
leads.text:
UNITED STATES COURT OF APPEALS FOR THE 
THIRD CIRCUIT 
No. 25-2006 
LISA DEBAR, Individually and as personal representative of 
the Estate of Cody Hatt, 
Appellant 

v. 

FIRSTENERGY CORP.; FIRSTENERGY GENERATION LLC; 
FIRSTENERGY SOLUTIONS CORP.; FIRSTENERGY 
PENNSYLV ANIA ELECTRIC CO.; FIRSTENERGY SERVICE CO.; ET 
AL. 

AMENDED PURSUANT TO CLERKS ORDER DA TED 7/14/25 
_____________________________ 
On Appeal from the U.S. District Court, E.D. Pa. 
Chief Judge Wendy Beetlestone, No. 2:24-cv-05164 

Before: RESTREPO, BIBAS, and FISHER, Circuit Judges 
Argued: Apr. 20, 2026; Filed: Oct. 14, 2026 
_____________________________ 
OPINION OF THE COURT 
FISHER, Circuit Judge. 

2 
Cody Hatt suffered fatal injuries while working for a 
demolition contractor that was tearing down a power plant in 
Pennsylvania known as Hatfield’s Ferry . His mother, as his 
survivor and on behalf of his estate, sued the owner and 
operators of the plant for negligence . T he District Court 
dismissed the complaint. 
Two Pennsylvania tort law doctrines govern this appeal. 
First, when a property owner hires an independent contractor 
to work on the property, the owner does not owe a duty to 
employees of the contractor. There is an exception when the 
owner hires a contractor but retains detailed control over the 
job—over not only what is to be done, but how and by whom. 
The retained-control exception is difficult to show ; an owner 
does not retain control by imposing safety requirements or 
contract specifications for the work. Here, the plaintiff has not 
alleged facts that, if true, would demonstrate that the 
defendants retained sufficient control . The second applicable 
tort law doctrine is that a landowner has no duty to protect 
those invited onto its land from dangers that are open and 
obvious. The risks of demolishing the long-disused Hatfield’s 
Ferry Power Station were indeed obvious, and the complaint 
fails to allege otherwise. We will therefore affirm. 
I. 
A. Which documents we consider 
At the outset, we confront the question of what parts of 
the record to consider on appeal . When ruling on a motion to 
dismiss, “courts may consider documents integral to or 
explicitly relied upon in the complaint, or any undisputedly 

3 
authentic document that a defendant attaches . . . to a motion 
to dismiss if the plaintiff’s claims are based on the document.” 
In re Asbestos Prod. Liab. Litig. (No. VI) , 822 F.3d 125, 133 
n.7 (3d Cir. 2016) (citation modified). The parties attached five 
documents to the complaint and the motion to dismiss. All of 
them are within bounds for us to consider, but we rely primarily 
on the two about which DeBar has expressed no objection: the 
demolition contract and the Specification. 
The demolition contract. DeBar attached to her 
complaint a document titled “Purchase Order,” which was the 
demolition contract between North American Dismantling and 
FirstEnergy Service. The District Court took this document 
into account, and correctly so: the demolition contract is 
“integral to or explicitly relied upon in the complaint.” In re 
Asbestos Prod., 822 F.3d at 133 n.7. 
The Specification. DeBar alleged that FirstEnergy 
Service created the “Generation Specification of the Hatfield 
Power Plant . . . , which set forth detailed specifications for 
how the demolition work was to be performed .” App. 965 . 
FirstEnergy Service attached to its motion to dismiss a 
document title d “FIRSTENERGY GENERATION, LLC 
SPECIFICATION FLT -SPEC-XX-XXXX FOR 
DEMOLITION OF HATFIELD POWER PLANT,” App. 
1052. The District Court did not consider this document 
because its title does not exactly match the references in the 
complaint. But i f the mismatch created doubt, DeBar has 
cleared it up on appeal : in her brief, she cites FirstEnergy’s 
Specification document, treating it as a source of information 
about the parties’ contract. In other words, she does not dispute 

4 
the Specification’s authenticity. Additionally, DeBar’s claims 
are based on this document , which outlines FirstEnergy’s 
requirements for the demolition project . So we will consider 
the Specification. 
The remaining documents. DeBar referenced two other 
documents in the complaint but did not attach them: the “FE 
Generation Personal Safety Manual” and the FirstEnergy 
Service “Code of Conduct.” App. 966. It is unclear whether 
either of these documents is among the three FirstEnergy 
attached to its motion to dismiss : the “Preliminary Work Plan 
for FirstEnergy – Demolition, Hatfield Power Plant,” App. 
1137; North American Dismantling’s “Environmental, Health, 
Safety and Security Plan and Manual for FirstEnergy Hatfield 
Power Plant,” id. at 1169; and the “North American 
Dismantling Corp. Safety Program,” id. at 1194. Even if these 
attachments are not the documents DeBar referenced in the 
complaint, we still may consider them if they are “undisputedly 
authentic” and DeBar’s “claims are based on [them].” In re 
Asbestos Prod., 822 F.3d at 133 n.7. 
DeBar has not question ed the authenticity of the 
documents. And her claims are based on the documents, 
because—like the demolition contract and Specification—they 
lay out the duties of FirstEnergy Service and North American 
Dismantling with regard to the Hatfield ’s Ferry demolition 
project. So we may take these attachments into account as well. 
In the District Court, DeBar complained that 
FirstEnergy Service “carefully controlled the documents . . . 
that it wishe [d] for the Court to consider, ” providing some 
“while holding back others .” App. 1668 n.2. Even without 

5 
considering the “Preliminary Work Plan,” the “Environmental, 
Health, Safety and Security Plan, ” and the “North American 
Dismantling Corp. Safety Program” —the documents 
FirstEnergy Service “wishe[d] for the Court to consider,” id.—
the complaint fails to state a claim.1 
B. Factual and procedural history 
1. The plant and the contract 
Allegheny Energy Supply owned a coal -fired power 
plant, the Hatfield’s Ferry Power Station, in Carmichaels, 
Pennsylvania. The plant was operated by FirstEnergy Corp. 
and FirstEnergy Service. In 2013, FirstEnergy Corp. and 
FirstEnergy Service , under pressure from the Environmental 
Protection Agency, decided to shut down coal generation at 
Hatfield’s Ferry . In 2022, demolition of the plant began —
including its two cooling towers, which were around 500 feet 
high, and its three emissions stacks, which ranged from 540 to 
700-plus feet. 
FirstEnergy Service contracted with North American 
Dismantling to complete more than $4 million worth of 
demolition work at the plant. FirstEnergy Service entered into 
the contract, titled a “Purchase Order,” “on its own behalf and 
on behalf of its affiliates,” who were not named. App. 1009. 
FirstEnergy assigned a buyer and a project manager to the 
project who used e-mail addresses with the domain 
“@firstenergycorp.com.” Id. at 1010. The Specification called 

1 Defendants argue persuasively that these documents 
further show that the District Court correctly dismissed the 
complaint. See Appellee’s Br. 9–13, 40–41. 

6 
for a “Purchaser’s Engineer” to serve as “the designated 
Engineering Representative from the Project Engineering 
Department, FirstEnergy Corp.” Id. at 1056. North American 
Dismantling was to submit invoices “electronically at the 
FirstEnergy Supplier Portal,” which had a 
“firstenergycorp.com” web address, and to direct payment 
questions to an e-mail address with the 
“@firstenergycorp.com” domain. Id. at 1010. 
The contract provided that the demolition work was to 
be performed “in accordance with [FirstEnergy’s] Generation 
Specification of Hatfield Power Plant.” Id. at 1010. 
FirstEnergy Service had “unobstructed access to Contractor’s 
or any of its Subcontractors’ Work, facilities, procedures and 
records for the purpose of observing and reviewing Work 
completion and quality.” Id. at 1014. The work was “subject to 
[FirstEnergy Service’s] inspection, tests, and count at any time 
or place at [FirstEnergy Service’s] discretion.” Id. North 
American Dismantling’s employees working at Hatfield were 
“subject to [FirstEnergy Service’s] continuing approval,” and 
FirstEnergy Service retained the right to “object to any [North 
American Dismantling] employee who, in [FirstEnergy 
Service’s] opinion, did not meet” the contract criteria “or 
whose performance [was] unsatisfactory.” Id. at 1015. If 
FirstEnergy Service objected to a North American Dismantling 
employee, North American Dismantling was required to 
“immediately replace or remove such individual.” Id. 
For its part, North American Dismantling agreed that it 
would be “considered an independent contractor . . . 
responsible for all acts and omissions (negligent or otherwise) 

7 
of its agents, employees and subcontractors.” Id. at 1013. North 
American Dismantling was “alone . . . liable and responsible 
for the manner and methods by which the Work [was] 
performed and for materials, work force and equipment.” Id. 
North American Dismantling “assume[d] full responsibility for 
[its] employees’ acts and omissions (negligent or otherwise)” 
and was required to “enforce all . . . worker health and safety 
and similar requirements.” Id. at 1015. 
With regard to safety, North American Dismantling 
agreed it was “solely responsible for the safety and health of 
its employees” and would “conduct the Work in a manner to 
avoid risk of bodily harm to persons or damage to property.” 
Id. at 1016. North American Dismantling further committed to 
“take all necessary safety and health precautions, and . . . do 
everything necessary to prevent accidents or injury to persons 
on . . . the premises.” Id. In addition, it would “not require any 
employee . . . to work in surroundings or under working 
conditions that [were] . . . hazardous, or dangerous to safety or 
health.” Id. 
North American Dismantling also agreed that it had 
“examined the site in all ways pertinent to performance 
required by the Specification, and that it [had] informed itself 
concerning the physical and geological conditions to be 
encountered . . . [and] the character of the Work to be 
performed.” Id. at 1027. The Specification further provided 
that FirstEnergy Service “assume[d] no responsibility for 
buildings and structures to be Demolished. Conditions existing 
at time of inspection for bidding purpose [would] be 
maintained by [FirstEnergy Service] as far as practical.” Id. at 

8 
1082. 
Drawing on the contract documents, DeBar alleged that 
FirstEnergy Service “exerted actual control over the 
[demolition] work by instructing and/or directing [North 
American Dismantling]” where, when, by what means, and 
with what equipment to do the work and by “giving 
instructions and/or directi ons to [North American 
Dismantling] personnel as to the manner of doing the actual 
demolition work.” Id. at 965. DeBar also alleged that 
FirstEnergy Service required North American Dismantling to 
comply with a “Code of Conduct” and with the Specification 
document, which “set forth detailed specifications for how the 
demolition work was to be performed.” Id. 
To further support her allegations that FirstEnergy 
Service actually controlled the work, DeBar invoked the “FE 
Generation Personal Safety Manual.” Id. at 966. And she noted 
the assignment to the project of the FirstEnergy Service project 
manager and purchaser representative, who oversaw 
“contracted personnel to assure compliance with the contract 
documents . . . , field construction work and continuous 
monitoring of project safety.” Id. at 966, 967. She alleged that 
when North American Dismantling “elected to or intended to 
do the work in a manner inconsistent with how [FirstEnergy 
Service] dictated” in the Specification, Personal Safety 
Manual, and Code of Conduct, FirstEnergy Service “ forced 
strict compliance with [those] documents, thereby exerting 
actual control.” Id. at 967.

In the 
United States Court of Appeals 
For the Eleventh Circuit 
____________________

____________________ 

ATTORNEY GENERAL, STATE OF FLORIDA, 
DEPARTMENT OF LEGAL AFFAIRS, 
Plaintiﬀ-Appellant, 
versus 

SNAP INC., 
Defendant-Appellee. 
 ____________________ 
Appeal from the United States District Court 
for the Northern District of Florida 
D.C. Docket No. 3:25-cv-00676-MW-HTC 
____________________ 

Before NEWSOM, LUCK, and TJOFLAT, Circuit Judges. 
PER CURIAM: 
With the rise of social media usage comes concern about its 
impact on the mental health of its users, particularly adolescents. 
In response to this growing concern, Florida’s legislature enacted a 
USCA11 Case: 25-12814 Document: 64-1 Date Filed: 10/14/2026 Page: 1 of 23 
2 Opinion of the Court 25-12814 
law to regulate social media platforms that use addictive features. 
This case arises from the State’s attempt to enforce that law. While 
the law raises serious constitutional questions, we do not reach 
them because the District Court lacked subject matter jurisdiction 
over this case. 
I. BACKGROUND 
The Florida legislature enacted House Bill 3 (“HB3”) in 2024. 
H.B. 3, 2024 Leg., Reg. Sess. (Fla. 2024) (codified in relevant part in 
Fla. Stat. § 501.1736). HB3 requires qualifying social media plat-
forms to prohibit minors from entering contracts to become ac-
count holders.1 Id. § 501.1736(2)(1). A social media platform quali-
fies under the statute if it meets certain criteria and employs one of 
five “addictive” features.2 

1 The law requires platforms to prohibit minors younger than 14 from becom-
ing account holders. Fla. Stat. § 501.1736(2)(a)–(b)(1). It allows minors aged 14 
or 15 to become account holders with consent from the minor’s parent or 
guardian. Id. § 501.1736(3)(a)–(b)(1). 
2 Section 501.1736 states, in relevant part: 
(e) “Social media platform” means an online forum, website, 
or application that satisfies each of the following criteria: 
1. Allows users to upload content or view the content or activ-
ity of other users; 
2. Ten percent or more of the daily users who are younger 
than 16 years of age spend on average 2 hours per day or longer 
on the online forum, website, or application on the days when 
using the online forum, website or application during the pre-
vious 12 months or, if the online forum, website, or application 
USCA11 Case: 25-12814 Document: 64-1 Date Filed: 10/14/2026 Page: 2 of 23 
25-12814 Opinion of the Court 3 
 The statute went into effect on January 1, 2025, authorizing 
the Office of the Attorney General’s Department of Legal Affairs 
(the “Department”) to bring civil actions to enforce HB3 against 
qualifying platforms and impose monetary sanctions “of up to 

did not exist during the previous 12 months, during the previ-
ous month; 
3. Employs algorithms that analyze user data or information 
on users to select content for users; and 
4. Has any of the following addictive features: 
a. Infinite scrolling, which means either: 
(I) Continuously loading content, or content that loads as the 
user scrolls down the page without the need to open a separate 
page; or 
(II) Seamless content, or the use of pages with no visible or 
apparent end or page breaks. 
b. Push notifications or alerts sent by the online forum, web-
site, or application to inform a user about specific activities or 
events related to the user’s account. 
c. Displays personal interactive metrics that indicate the num-
ber of times other users have clicked a button to indicate their 
reaction to content or have shared or reposted the content. 
d. Auto-play video or video that begins to play without the 
user first clicking on the video or on a play button for that 
video. 
e. Live-streaming or a function that allows a user or advertiser 
to broadcast live video content in real-time. 
Fla. Stat. § 501.1736(1)(e) 
USCA11 Case: 25-12814 Document: 64-1 Date Filed: 10/14/2026 Page: 3 of 23 
4 Opinion of the Court 25-12814 
$50,000 per violation” and, in some cases, punitive damages. 
Fla. Stat. § 501.1736(5). 
 In April 2025, the Department brought such an enforcement 
action against Snap Inc., the operator of the popular social media 
platform known as Snapchat. The complaint alleged Snap, a quali-
fying platform under the statute, was “openly defying” HB3 by 
contracting with minors under the age of 14. The Department sued 
Snap in Florida state court for violating HB3 and the Florida De-
ceptive and Unfair Trade Practices Act (“FDUTPA”) . It sought, 
among other things, injunctive relief, civil penalties, and punitive 
damages. 
A. Removal to Federal Court 
 Snap filed a notice of removal in the Northern District of 
Florida, arguing the Court had subject matter jurisdiction pursuant 
to 28 U.S.C. § 1332(a) and the federal officer removal statute, which 
allows removal of actions against any person “acting under [a fed-
eral] officer . . . for or relating to any act under color of such office.” 
28 U.S.C. § 1442(a)(1). The Department moved for remand. 
1. Federal Officer Removal 
 Snap argued the Department’s claims were removable un-
der the federal officer removal statute because Snap provided ad-
vertising services to two federal agencies: the Department of 
Homeland Security (“DHS”) and the Food and Drug Administra-
tion (“FDA”). It asserted the Department’s claims “interfere with 
Snap’s ability to carry out its responsibilities” under DHS and FDA 
USCA11 Case: 25-12814 Document: 64-1 Date Filed: 10/14/2026 Page: 4 of 23 
25-12814 Opinion of the Court 5 
officers, and it argued HB3 “would penalize Snap for its work as-
sisting the federal government in accomplishing its goals of reach-
ing teenage audiences” with the advertisements. 
 Snap purportedly entered into memorandums of under-
standing (“MOUs”) with DHS’s Cyber Crimes Center and Child 
Exploitation Investigations Unit to help DHS develop its 
“Know2Protect” campaign —a public safety initiative directed at 
educating teenagers and adults about online safety and preventing 
child sexual exploitation and abuse.3 DHS purportedly handpicked 
Snap to help carry out the campaign because of the platform’s abil-
ity to reach “one of the campaign’s key audiences: teens.” Under 
the MOUs, Snap conducted research on young adults’ awareness 
of child exploitation risks and devel oped advertising features to 
“bring important online safety information to [the teen] commu-
nity directly.” 
 Similarly, Snap contends that it assist ed with public health 
campaigns for the FDA’s Center for Tobacco Products. The cam-
paigns targeted audiences of 13 to 17 with messages about the risks 
of vaping and cigarette use.4 The FDA contracted with a third-party 
media agency to create advertising campaigns with SNAP. Specifi-
cally, in the lead up to the FDA’s 2025 campaigns, the marketing 
agency provided Snap with briefs explaining the FDA’s goals for 

3 Snap states that DHS carries out the Know2Protect campaign in furtherance 
of its child exploitation prevention responsibilities under 6 U.S.C. § 473. 
4 Snap alleged that the FDA carried out this advertisement campaign pursuant 
to its duties under 21 U.S.C. §§ 393(d)(2)(D) and 387a(e). 
USCA11 Case: 25-12814 Document: 64-1 Date Filed: 10/14/2026 Page: 5 of 23 
6 Opinion of the Court 25-12814 
the campaigns. Snap then submitted proposals for the campaigns 
and explained how its proprietary algorithms could help the FDA 
reach their intended audience. After receiving FDA approval, the 
marketing agency purchased advertising from Snap for one of the 
campaigns. 
 The Department moved to remand, arguing (1) Snap’s 
“brief partnership[s]” with DHS, the FDA, and their contractors 
came “nowhere near the deep and enduring ties, control, and su-
pervision” required to establish Snap “act[ed] under” a federal of-
ficer, (2) Snap failed to provide any evidence to support its allega-
tions of federal officer jurisdiction, and (3) Snap failed to show that 
the conduct for which it was being sued was performed under color 
of federal law. 
2. Diversity Jurisdiction 
 Snap also argued the Department’s claims were removable 
under diversity jurisdiction. Because the relief the Department 
sought was “allegedly for the direct benefit of identifiable, individ-
ual Florida citizens,” Snap argued “the citizenship of those individ-
uals control[led] for the purposes of diversity.” 
 In its motion for remand, the Department responded that it 
brought the suit pursuant to its statutory mandate to enforce the 
laws at issue. It also pointed out that it sought injunctive and puni-
tive relief, making clear the aim of the suit was to bring a benefit to 
the State by “deterring future violations by Snap or other wrong-
doers.” The Department contended that this meant the interested 
party was the State of Florida. 
USCA11 Case: 25-12814 Document: 64-1 Date Filed: 10/14/2026 Page: 6 of 23 
25-12814 Opinion of the Court 7 
B. The Department’s Motion for Temporary Injunction 
 The Department also asked the District Court to temporar-
ily enjoin Snap from violating HB3. It argued the Attorney General 
had a legal right to an injunction because Snap was openly violating 
HB3 and the enforcement of HB3 does not violate the First Amend-
ment. 
 Snap responded that the Department’s injunction argument 
was foreclosed by the District Court ’s recent order in Comput. & 
Commc’ns Indus. Ass’n v. Uthmeier , 826 F.Supp.3d 1358 (N.D. Fla. 
2025) (“CCIA”). In that case, which was filed prior to the instant 
suit, two nonprofit associations representing internet and technol-
ogy companies sued for a declaration that HB3 violates the First 
Amendment and sought preliminary and permanent injunctions 
barring the Florida Attorney General from enforcing it. Id. The Dis-
trict Court found HB3 is likely unconstitutional and preliminary 
enjoined its enforcement.
5 Id. at 1390. 
 Snap also argued the Department failed to show a likelihood 
of success on the merits because HB3 violates the First Amend-
ment and the Commerce Clause and is preempted by the Chil-
dren’s Online Privacy Protection Act. 

5 That decision is currently on appeal before this Court. 
USCA11 Case: 25-12814 Document: 64-1 Date Filed: 10/14/2026 Page: 7 of 23 
8 Opinion of the Court 25-12814 
* * * 
 The District Court sided with Snap on both motions. It de-
nied the Department’s motion to remand, finding that Snap estab-
lished the three elements required for federal officer removal based 
on its relationships with DHS and the FDA. It also denied the De-
partment’s motion for temporary injunction, relying on its finding 
in CCIA that HB3 was likely unconstitutional. The Department 
timely appeals both denials. 
II. DISCUSSION 
 This case requires us to answer three questions: (1) Do we 
have jurisdiction to hear this appeal? (2) Was the case properly re-
moved to federal court under the federal officer removal statute? 
(3) And, if not, is additional fact-finding required to determine if the 
case was properly removed to federal court under diversity juris-
diction? We answer each question in turn. 
A. Appellate Jurisdiction 
 We are obligated to inquire sua sponte into our own juris-
diction to hear an appeal. Thomas v. Blue Cross & Blue Shield Ass’n , 
594 F.3d 814, 818 (11th Cir. 2010). Appellate courts have jurisdic-
tion over appeals of final orders of the district courts and certain 
nonfinal orders, including those denying injunctions. 28 U.S.C. 
§§ 1291, 1292(a)(1). Congress specifically vested appellate courts 
with jurisdiction over appeals of orders remanding cases to state 
court pursuant to the federal officer removal statute. Id. §§ 1447(d), 
1442. However, Congress is silent as to whether we have jurisdic-
tion over appeals of orders denying such remands. While “such an
